title: Al Bar del Corso
subtitle: At the Bar del Corso
intro: Seven thirty, five people at the counter, no queue. You order at the wrong place, pay at the wrong moment, and get a nickname. In this unit you learn how an Italian bar works, how to order and pay, how to say what you like, and your first full set of regular verbs.
objectives: Order food and drink at a bar and ask how much it costs
Use the regular [[-are]] verbs in all six persons: [[parlo]], [[mangi]], [[paga]]…
Say what you like with [[mi piace]] and [[mi piacciono]]
Count to a thousand and beyond, and understand prices in euros and cents
Use [[anche]], [[solo]], [[ancora]] and [[già]] in the right place
canDo: A1 · Spoken interaction: can order food and drink using simple phrases and ask how much something costs.
A1 · Spoken interaction: can say what they like and dislike in simple terms.
A1 · Listening: can understand prices and simple questions in a service situation when spoken slowly.
A1 · Reading: can understand a simple price list or menu.
A1 · Spoken production: can describe daily habits with very simple sentences (I work, I eat, I speak).

sections.title: Cassa, scontrino, bancone
sections.intro: Two scenes at Nando's bar: the first coffee, done wrong and then right, and Pasquale's breakfast lesson. Listen for the prices.

blocks.title: Al bancone
blocks.setting: Bar del Corso, ore 7:30. Al bancone cinque persone, nessuna fila. Nando è dietro la macchina del caffè; Rita, sua moglie, è alla cassa.

lines.t: Buongiorno! Un cappuccino, per favore.
lines.n: Good morning! A cappuccino, please.

lines.t: Buongiorno! Lo scontrino?
lines.n: Good morning! The receipt?

lines.t: Lo scontrino? Ma… pago dopo?
lines.n: The receipt? But… do I pay afterwards?

lines.t: No, prima. Cassa, scontrino, bancone. In quest'ordine.
lines.n: No, first. Till, receipt, counter. In that order.

lines.t: Ho capito, scusi. Un cappuccino e un cornetto. Quant'è?
lines.n: Got it, sorry. A cappuccino and a croissant. How much is it?
lines.note: At the till, to Rita. Quant'è? is the question for the total; quanto costa? asks the price of one thing.

lines.t: Due e cinquanta.
lines.n: Two fifty.
lines.note: Prices are said without euro: due e cinquanta = €2.50.

lines.t: Ecco. … Ecco lo scontrino!
lines.n: Here. … Here's the receipt!

t.m: Bravo! Cappuccino e cornetto. Tu sei il nipote di Cosimo, no? Il canadese!
t.f: Brava! Cappuccino e cornetto. Tu sei la nipote di Cosimo, no? La canadese!
t.note: Bravo / brava agrees, and so does the nickname: il canadese for Luca, la canadese for Lucia. Canadese itself doesn't change; the article does the work.

lines.n: Well done! Cappuccino and croissant. You're Cosimo's grandchild, right? The Canadian!

lines.t: Sì! Ma come lo sa?
lines.n: Yes! But how do you know?
lines.note: The protagonist keeps Lei with Nando for now (lo sa). Nando uses tu with everyone.

lines.t: Roccamarina è piccola. Io sono Nando. Qui lavoro dalle sei alle otto di sera. Zucchero?
lines.n: Roccamarina is small. I'm Nando. I work here from six to eight at night. Sugar?

lines.t: No, grazie. Lei… tu… parli inglese?
lines.n: No, thanks. Do you (Lei… tu…) speak English?

lines.t: "Yes, a little." Scherzo! Un po'. I turisti ordinano, io capisco. Mangi al bancone o al tavolo?
lines.n: "Yes, a little." Joking! A bit. The tourists order, I understand. Are you eating at the counter or at a table?

lines.t: Che differenza c'è?
lines.n: What's the difference?

lines.t: Al tavolo costa di più. Al bancone costa meno, e parli con me.
lines.n: At a table it costs more. At the counter it costs less, and you talk to me.

lines.t: Al bancone, allora.
lines.n: At the counter, then.

notes.note: How much is it (all together)? Quanto + è. The answer comes without the word euro: tre e venti.
The receipt from the till. At most bars you pay first, then show it at the counter. See Living there.
Just kidding! From scherzare, to joke. Nando's favourite word.
It costs more / it costs less. Comparisons arrive in unit 10; these two are useful now.

blocks.title: Offro io
blocks.setting: Ore 8. Entra Pasquale con il giornale sotto il braccio.

t.m: Buongiorno, Nando. Buongiorno, canadese. Un caffè. E cosa prende il nipote di Cosimo?
t.f: Buongiorno, Nando. Buongiorno, canadese. Un caffè. E cosa prende la nipote di Cosimo?

lines.n: Good morning, Nando. Good morning, Canadian. A coffee. And what's Cosimo's grandchild having?
lines.note: Cosa prende? (Lei form) is the question you will hear in every bar and restaurant: what are you having?

lines.t: Niente, grazie. Ho già il cappuccino.
lines.n: Nothing, thanks. I already have my cappuccino.

lines.t: Allora un altro cornetto. Offro io.
lines.n: Then another croissant. My treat.

lines.t: Grazie, professore. Ma non mangio molto la mattina.
lines.n: Thank you, professor. But I don't eat much in the morning.

lines.t: In Italia la colazione è piccola: un caffè, un cornetto. Non uova e pancetta.
lines.n: In Italy breakfast is small: a coffee, a croissant. Not eggs and bacon.

lines.t: Il professore paga, tu mangi. Qui funziona così.
lines.n: The professor pays, you eat. That's how it works here.

lines.t: Allora grazie. Un cornetto alla crema.
lines.n: Then thank you. A cream croissant.

lines.t: Nando, quant'è?
lines.n: Nando, how much is it?

lines.t: Due e venti. Professore, il caffè costa un euro e dieci, come sempre.
lines.n: Two twenty. Professor, the coffee is one euro ten, like always.

lines.t: Nel 1985 costava trecento lire.
lines.n: In 1985 it cost three hundred lire.
lines.note: Costava: "it used to cost", the imperfetto of unit 11. Pasquale remembers every price since the lira.

notes.note: I'm paying, it's on me. Literally "I offer". The reply is grazie, not a fight over the bill: that comes later, when you know each other.
That's how it works here. The sentence that explains Italy.
Cream-filled. Also al cioccolato, alla marmellata, vuoto (plain). Alla / al = "with" for fillings and flavours.

questions.q: How much is a coffee at the Bar del Corso?
questions.why: Un euro e dieci, come sempre. The 300 lire was 1985.

sections.title: Al bar
sections.intro: What you drink, what you eat, how you pay, and twelve regular -are verbs that run your day. Say the drinks aloud: cappuccino has two double consonants, and the Pronunciation section is about exactly that.

items.note: Always an espresso. A long one is un caffè lungo; with a drop of milk, un caffè macchiato.

ex.t: Il cappuccino è una cosa da mattina.
Un latte? Un bicchiere di latte freddo?

ex.t: Un tè al limone, per favore.

items.note: With the accent: tè. Without it, te means "you".
You will be asked this at every table in Italy.
Il succo is bottled juice; la spremuta is squeezed in front of you.

ex.t: Un cornetto alla crema o vuoto?

items.note: Cornetto in the centre and south, brioche in the north. Both are sweeter and softer than a French croissant.

ex.t: Un panino con prosciutto e formaggio.

items.note: One panino, two panini. "A panini" is a Canadian mistake.

ex.t: I tramezzini sono per il pranzo veloce.
ex.n: Tramezzini are for a quick lunch.

items.note: Lo zucchero: z takes lo. Amaro = no sugar.

ex.n: I have breakfast at the bar.

items.note: Fare colazione = to have breakfast. Dialect and the north say also prima colazione.

ex.t: A Roccamarina la cena è alle nove.
ex.n: In Roccamarina dinner is at nine.

items.note: Soft c: "CHEH-na".

ex.t: Prima lo scontrino, poi il caffè.
ex.n: First the receipt, then the coffee.
At the counter it costs less.
At a table it costs more.

items.note: Il tavolino is the little café table outside.

ex.n: The prices are on the price list.

items.note: Invariable: un euro, dieci euro. Never euri.
Usually dropped: un euro e dieci.
Tenga il resto = keep the change (rare in a bar).
Pago in contanti = I pay cash.
Also paper, and a playing card. Il bancomat is the debit card and the ATM.

ex.t: In Italia la mancia non è obbligatoria.
ex.n: In Italy a tip is not expected.

ex.t: Il listino è sopra la cassa.
ex.n: The price list is above the till.

blocks.intro: All regular. Learn the infinitive and the io form; the rest follows the pattern in How it works.

ex.t: Parlo inglese e un po' di italiano.
ex.n: I speak English and a little Italian.
I don't eat much in the morning.

items.note: Tu mangi, with one i.
Tu paghi, with an h.

ex.t: Nando lavora dalle sei alle otto di sera.
ex.n: Nando works from six to eight at night.
I live on Via delle Rose.

items.note: For where you live. Vivere (to live, to be alive) is unit 4.

ex.n: I'm waiting for Dora at the bar.

items.note: No preposition: aspetto Dora, not aspetto per Dora.
Tu cerchi, with an h. No preposition: cerco un tavolo.

ex.n: I buy the bread at the bakery.

items.note: Tu studi, one i.

ex.t: Nando guarda la partita al bar.
ex.n: Nando watches the match at the bar.
I listen to the radio in the morning.

items.note: No preposition: ascolto la radio.

sections.title: I verbi in -are, e quanto costa
sections.intro: The first regular conjugation, the phrases that get you a coffee, the two forms of piacere, prices, and four little adverbs that go in a specific place. Reference pages at the end of each block.

blocks.title: Regular -are verbs: parlo, parli, parla
blocks.rule: Take off -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano. The stress stays on the stem in the loro form: PARlano, not parLAno.

blocks.caption: [[parlare]], [[mangiare]], [[pagare]] · presente
blocks.note: Mangiare: tu mangi, noi mangiamo (the i of the stem merges with the i of the ending). Pagare: tu paghi, noi paghiamo (the h keeps the hard g). The same goes for cercare → cerchi, giocare → giochi, studiare → studi, cominciare → cominci.

items.n: I work from six to eight.

items.t: Mangi al bancone o al tavolo?
items.n: Are you eating at the counter or at a table?
items.note: the present covers English "I eat", "I'm eating" and "I do eat"

items.n: We live on Via delle Rose.

items.t: I turisti ordinano in inglese e pagano in euro.
items.n: The tourists order in English and pay in euros.

blocks.title: One present, three English tenses
blocks.text: [[Mangio un cornetto.]] can mean *I eat a croissant*, *I'm eating a croissant* or *I do eat a croissant*. There is no separate continuous tense you need now ([[sto mangiando]] exists and comes in unit 12). The simple present does the work.

items.why: The loro form is stressed on the stem, like the io form. English speakers move the stress to the ending.
Spelling: -giare drops an i, -gare adds an h.

items.wrong: Aspetto per Dora. Cerco per un tavolo.
items.why: Aspettare, cercare, ascoltare, guardare take a direct object: no "for", no "to", no "at".

blocks.title: Ordering: vorrei, prendo, per me
blocks.rule: Three ways to order, all polite: vorrei (I'd like), prendo (I'll have), per me (for me). Then quant'è? for the total.

head: You say
English
Note
rows: vorrei is a form of volere (unit 14); for now, a fixed polite phrase
literally "I take": the most common way
Per me un tè, per lui un caffè.
A tea for me, a coffee for him.
one item; plural: quanto costano i cornetti?

blocks.caption: What they say to you
head: They say
English
rows: Yes? What can I get you? (informal / formal)
At the counter or at a table?

items.right: Un caffè, per favore. / Vorrei un caffè.
items.why: Grammatical but heavy. Italians order with the noun, prendo or vorrei; "can I have" is an English habit.

items.wrong: Un latte, per favore. (expecting a latte)
items.why: Un latte is a glass of milk.
Elided, always.

blocks.title: mi piace, mi piacciono
blocks.rule: To say you like something: mi piace + singular, mi piacciono + plural. The thing you like is the subject; you are the one it "is pleasing to".

head: singular thing
plural things
an activity
blocks.note: Lui / lei / noi / voi / loro forms in unit 7.

items.t: Mi piace il cappuccino, ma non mi piace lo zucchero.
items.n: I like cappuccino, but I don't like sugar.

items.t: Ti piacciono i cornetti alla crema? — Molto!
items.n: Do you like cream croissants? — Very much!

items.note: piace + infinitive, always singular

blocks.title: Why piacciono
blocks.text: Literally [[mi piacciono i cornetti]] is "croissants are pleasing to me": the croissants are the subject, so the verb is plural. Think of English "it pleases me / they please me" and the forms stop looking strange.

items.why: Plural thing, plural verb.
Io piaccio means "I am likeable". The liker is mi.
An infinitive counts as singular.

blocks.title: Numbers to 1,000 and beyond; prices
blocks.rule: cento, duecento… novecento; mille, duemila… ; un milione. Prices: euro invariable, cents after e, usually without the words euro and centesimi.

blocks.note: Cento never changes; mille becomes -mila in the plural. Italian writes thousands with a dot and decimals with a comma: 1.250,50.

items.t: L'affitto è quattrocentocinquanta euro al mese.
items.n: The rent is 450 euros a month.

items.t: Nel millenovecentottantacinque il caffè costava trecento lire.
items.note: years are read as full numbers

items.why: Euro is invariable.
Mille → -mila in compounds.

items.right: due euro e cinquanta / due e cinquanta
items.why: The e joins euros and cents.
No "one" before cento or mille: cento, mille.

blocks.title: anche, solo, ancora, già
blocks.rule: Anche (also) goes before the word it refers to; solo (only) too. Ancora (still, yet) and già (already) go after the verb.

items.note: anche + the thing it refers to (io)

items.n: I'll have a croissant as well.
items.note: anche before cornetto: the croissant is the extra

items.t: Non pago ancora? — No, ancora no.
items.n: Don't I pay yet? — No, not yet.

head: Adverb
Meaning
Position
rows: right before the word it adds to
right before the word it limits
after the verb; before an adjective

items.right: Anche io prendo un caffè. / Prendo anche un caffè.
items.why: Anche does not go at the end; where you put it changes what it refers to.
Già follows the verb.

items.wrong: Non ho ancora fame? (meaning "I'm still hungry")
items.why: Non… ancora = not yet; ancora without non = still.

sections.title: Le doppie
sections.intro: The number one problem for English speakers. A double consonant is held longer, and the vowel before it is shorter. It is never decoration: pala is a shovel, palla is a ball.

blocks.caption: Single or double? The meaning changes

pairs.tip: Nonno is the one you have. Get it right at Sunday lunch.
The one you need today: si paga alla cassa, not alla casa.

blocks.title: How to make a double
blocks.text: Stop on the consonant and hold it for a beat before letting go: cap-PUC-cino, not "capuchino". For p, t, c, hold the closure (silence) longer. For l, m, n, r, s, keep the sound going longer. The vowel before a double is short and sharp: the *a* of [[palla]] is shorter than the *a* of [[pala]]. If it feels exaggerated, it is right.

items.tip: Two doubles in one word. Hold the p, then hold the ch.
LAT-te: the t is held. English "latte" has no double.
PIT-tsa, with a long stop. Never "pee-za".
Hold the l with the tongue on the ridge.
A longer trill than the single r of caro.

items.t: Un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore. Sette e cinquanta? No, due e cinquanta.
items.n: A cappuccino and a croissant, please. Seven fifty? No, two fifty.
items.note: cappuccino · cornetto · sette: three doubles to hold

items.t: Nonno Cosimo pagava alla cassa, non alla casa.
items.n: Grandpa Cosimo paid at the till, not at the house.

sections.title: Come funziona un bar
sections.intro: The bar is where Italy starts its day, settles its arguments and keeps its gossip. A few rules nobody writes down.

blocks.text:
In most bars, especially busy ones and in cities, you pay first at the [[cassa]], get the [[scontrino]], then go to the [[bancone]] and order showing the receipt (or putting it on the counter with a coin on it, if you want to leave a small tip). In a small-town bar like Nando's, the regulars order first and pay when they leave, and the barista keeps the account in his head. When in doubt, look at what the person in front of you does, or ask: [[Pago prima o dopo?|Do I pay before or after?]]

The receipt is also a legal thing: the bar must give it to you, and in theory you must keep it until you leave. Nobody checks any more, but the habit remains.

Standing at the counter is the normal way to have a coffee: one minute, a word with the barista, done. Sitting at a table, especially outside, is a service and costs more, sometimes twice as much; the price list shows both ([[banco]] and [[tavolo]]). Nobody will hurry you at a table, and you can sit for an hour with one coffee. Nobody will stop you standing at the counter for an hour either, if the conversation is good.

blocks.title: The coffee menu
blocks.text: [[un caffè]]: an espresso · [[un caffè lungo]]: a bit longer · [[un ristretto]]: shorter · [[un macchiato]]: with a drop of milk foam · [[un cappuccino]]: espresso, steamed milk, foam · [[un caffellatte]] / [[latte macchiato]]: mostly milk · [[un caffè corretto]]: with a shot of grappa or sambuca · [[un americano]]: espresso with hot water · [[un decaffeinato]] / [[un deca]] · [[un caffè d'orzo]]: barley, no caffeine · [[un caffè freddo]] or [[shakerato]]: cold, in summer. Milk after lunch is unusual: a cappuccino at four will not be refused, but it will be noticed.

Italian breakfast is small and sweet: a coffee or cappuccino and a cornetto, standing, in five minutes, at home or at the bar. Eggs, bacon, cheese and anything salty belong to lunch. Sweet biscuits and milk at home are normal for children and adults alike. Pasquale is right about the eggs, and he is only slightly exaggerating about the lire: coffee was about 300 lire in the mid-eighties, roughly fifteen cents.

Paying for someone's coffee is a small, common gesture, and in a group someone usually pays for everyone and the next time someone else does. Accept with a [[grazie]] and return it another day. Splitting the bill at a bar is rare; splitting it at a restaurant, [[pagare alla romana]], is common among friends but not when someone has invited you. Tipping at the bar is not expected; leaving the small coins is enough and never required.

blocks.title: Il caffè sospeso
blocks.text: A Neapolitan tradition: you pay for two coffees and drink one; the second is "suspended" for someone who cannot afford it and asks for it later. Some bars elsewhere in Italy have adopted it. Nando's does, on a chalkboard by the till.
